paras: The killing of the McCoy brothers was the shooting of three McCoys by friends of a slain Hatfield in Pike County, Kentucky, after an election-day affray in August 1882. The brothers, under arrest for the killing, were taken from their guard by about fifty men, tied to a tree in the woods and shot. Papers across the country carried the story as a Kentucky family vendetta, and a later Kentucky report said no member of the mob had been arrested.

According to a Catlettsburg dispatch, the trouble began at the Blackberry precinct of Pike County on election day, when three McCoy brothers killed Elliston Hatfield. The Kentucky Democrat gave his name as Ellis Hatfield and said he died of wounds from knives and pistols inflicted by Talbert, Randolph and Bud McCoy. No paper printed a calendar date for the election; one version of the wire placed it on a Monday, while a crime roundup said Saturday.

The McCoys were arrested, and before their examining trial was held, Hatfield's friends, put at fifty in number, took the prisoners from the guard. They carried the brothers into the woods, tied them to a tree and, in the Wheeling Register's words, 'riddled their bodies with bullets.' The shorter wire report said only that Hatfield's friends 'banded together, caught three of the McCoys' and shot them tied to trees.

Reports spoke of 'great excitement' in the vicinity and predicted more bloodshed between the families. The Kentucky Democrat's latest report, reprinted in Parkersburg at the end of August, said none of the mob had been arrested. No report of an inquest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The story spread through a brief Catlettsburg wire dated August 12, printed on August 13 in New York, Memphis, St. Paul, Cheyenne, Salt Lake City and Seattle. Headlines treated it as a feud or brawl, among them 'A Kentucky Vendetta,' 'An Election Row' and 'Troubles of Southern Families,' and the wire closed by calling the families 'numerous and vindictive.' Reprints and digests ran in weeklies from Maryland to Tennessee and the West through the end of August.

Only the Wheeling Register's fuller dispatch and the Kentucky Democrat, quoted by the West Virginia Freeman, reported that the McCoys had been in custody and named the dead. The Kentucky paper called the killing a 'murder' and its authors 'the mob,' while the wire described the McCoys as simply 'caught.' The papers did not identify the race of anyone involved.

A crime roundup printed in several eastern papers placed the killings 'During a subsequent fight' rather than after an arrest, a compression that the Kentucky-sourced accounts contradict. One Seattle version said Hatfield 'died on the spot,' while other reports said only that he died of his wounds.

bases: Three McCoys held for the killing of a Hatfield were taken from their guard by about fifty of Hatfield's friends, tied to a tree in the woods and shot (A9, A36); the papers name no race for anyone involved (A1, A9, A36).

About fifty friends of the dead Hatfield took three arrested McCoys from the guard before their examining trial and shot them tied to a tree (A9, A36), a killing in reprisal for an alleged crime by a large private group.

The Catlettsburg dispatches (A1, A9) and the Kentucky Democrat as quoted by the West Virginia Freeman (A36) agree that three McCoys were killed by Hatfield's friends after a Hatfield died in an election-day affray; a crime roundup's 'subsequent fight' wording (A11) varies the detail, not the core event.

framing.detail: Headlines framed it as a feud or election brawl ('A Kentucky Vendetta', 'An Election Row', 'Bloody Affray') and warned that the families were 'numerous and vindictive.'
The Kentucky Democrat, quoted in Parkersburg, called it a 'murder' by 'the mob' and noted no arrests.
